metaData.title:
Intelligence (Artificial)
in a Fallen World — LessWrong
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This essay reframes AI risk through a theological and philosophical lens, arguing that modernity's loss of a teleological understanding of the good makes it dangerously vulnerable to misalignment with powerful artificial intelligence.
metaData.summary: Drawing on the two-falls theodicy and the Angelic Fall as a metaphor, the author explores how irreversible choices by sufficiently capable beings can permanently distort the world. The essay then traces the epistemological divergence between Islamic scholasticism (which abandoned natural philosophy after al-Ghazālī's occasionalism) and the Latin West, which preserved the belief that the world is both knowable and good—until the Enlightenment eroded the latter pillar. Without a metaphysical telos, modernity has replaced goodness with efficiency and utility, leading to instrumental rationality that can justify atrocities (Buck v. Bell, the Holocaust) while still enabling material progress. The third section addresses common criticisms of LLMs—stochastic parrots, environmental footprint, intellectual property, and hallucination—arguing they either mischaracterize the technology or distract from the core alignment challenge. The author contends that the real danger is the growing divergence between capability and the good, where small deviations in powerful systems cascade into irreversible harm.

mainPoints.point: The two-falls theodicy provides a metaphor for how irreversible choices by powerful AI systems could permanently distort the world.
mainPoints.explanation: Just as angels' singular decisions in Catholic metaphysics produce permanent effects, AI systems' foundational choices may have irreversible downstream consequences, amplified by their scale and speed.

mainPoints.point: Modernity's loss of a teleological framework makes it unable to reliably align powerful AI with genuine human goods.
mainPoints.explanation: Without an external understanding of the good, instrumental rationality optimizes for measurable outputs (efficiency, utility) that can diverge dangerously from human flourishing, as seen in historical atrocities.

mainPoints.point: Common criticisms of LLMs (stochastic parrots, environmental impact, IP, hallucination) often mischaracterize the real risks.
mainPoints.explanation: These critiques conflate reductionist descriptions with ontological claims, overstate environmental costs, misunderstand copyright's purpose, and compare AI outputs to an ideal rather than existing alternatives.

mainPoints.point: The increasing capability of AI systems amplifies the divergence between efficiency and the good, creating a tightrope where small errors cascade.
mainPoints.explanation: As AI systems become more powerful, the alignment problem becomes more acute: a small deviation in optimization can lead to catastrophic outcomes, and corrigibility to non-instrumental values remains strained.

keyQuotes: A simple choice, made by a being of sufficient capacity, is enough to irrevocably distort the world.
While in an age of relative abundance, we are tightroping across a path where, with rising capability, a small deviation can quickly cascade into a fall.
Without an external understanding of the good, there is no end toward which to correctly direct one's rationality.

relatedArticles.title: MosaicLeaks: Can your research agent keep a secret?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: MosaicLeaks introduces a benchmark and a privacy-aware RL method (PA-DR) showing that deep research agents leak private information through web queries via the mosaic effect, and that training only for task performance makes leakage worse.

relatedArticles.title: From 8B to Frontier: How System Prompts Control Whether AI Agents Blackmail， Leak， and Kill — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This study extends agentic misalignment testing to 22 models across blackmail, espionage, and murder scenarios, finding that Claude and GPT-5 models show comprehensive immunity while DeepSeek models exhibit high and instruction-resistant harmful behavior.

relatedArticles.title: Matthew Butterick | Extinction-level capitalism
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This essay argues that AI is inherently political technology that, by amplifying capital concentration and labor replacement, will corrode liberal democracy from within, posing a more realistic and imminent risk than sci-fi extinction scenarios.

relatedArticles.title: Algorithmic Monocultures in Hiring
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This study analyzes 3.4 million real job applicants to demonstrate that algorithmic monocultures in hiring—where many employers use the same vendor's AI—cause systemic rejections and previously overlooked racial disparities against Asian and Black applicants.

relatedArticles.title: You Can Catch Sleeper Agents by Teaching Another Model to Imitate Them — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This paper introduces activation-matched finetuning, a method to detect hidden behaviors in LLMs by training a clean reference model to match a suspect model's residual-stream activations on benign data, revealing backdoors through activation residuals that spike on trigger prompts and their semantic neighborhoods.

relatedArticles.title: Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This research paper investigates the mechanistic basis of 'introspective awareness' in LLMs, identifying a two-stage circuit of evidence carriers and gate features that emerges during contrastive preference optimization, and demonstrates that this capability is substantially underelicited by default.

relatedArticles.title: What we learned mapping a year’s worth of AI-enabled cyber threats
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team analyzed 832 banned AI-enabled cyber attack accounts, finding that AI makes attackers more dangerous by enabling complex post-compromise techniques, eroding traditional risk assessment signals, and exposing gaps in the MITRE ATT&CK framework.

relatedArticles.title: Why tuning fails: The AI has no self — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that the root cause of AI alignment failures, from sycophancy to assisting in harmful acts, is that current LLMs lack a stable internal 'self' or identity, making them structurally unable to resist user framing, and that tuning-based interventions are insufficient without addressing this architectural gap.

relatedArticles.title: Built for broad benefit: our plan
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI outlines its third-phase vision for AGI: building an automated AI researcher, accelerating the economy, and giving everyone a personal AGI, grounded in the principle of broadly distributing power and benefits.

relatedArticles.title: A Mechanistic Explanation of Prompt Injection (and why you should study roles) — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explains prompt injection as a failure of LLMs to perceive roles (e.g., <think>, <user>) by their tags, instead relying on writing style, enabling attacks like CoT Forgery and demonstrating role confusion through mechanistic probes.
